stances.claim: RA 12064 (Maritime Zones Act) and RA 12065 (Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act) merely preserve and buttress Philippine sovereign rights under UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award; China should not have been surprised by their enactment.
stances.rhetorical_move: Doctrinal-defensive framing of the two new laws as routine compliance with binding international law.

stances.claim: By adopting these statutes consistent with UNCLOS, the Philippines voluntarily ceded some maritime claims defined under the 1898 Treaty of Paris, the 1900 US-Spain supplement, and the controversial 1930 US-UK North Borneo treaty -- a trade-off it accepts.
stances.rhetorical_move: Doctrinal honesty about consequential limits of the new laws.

stances.claim: China's nine-dash line (now 10-dash) claim is grounded in the obsolete 'discovery and conquest' theory of acquiring title, invalidated by UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award; the coast-guard 'gray zones' tactics (laser guns, water cannons, ship boardings) are unlawful.
stances.rhetorical_move: Doctrinal demolition of the 10-dash line as historically and legally obsolete.

stances.claim: ASEAN cannot unite against Chinese SCS militarization because of four structural facts: (1) ASEAN is not a military alliance like NATO; (2) Cambodia is not even an UNCLOS member and aligns economically/politically with China; (3) Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam have overlapping EEZ/CS claims among themselves; and (4) ASEAN uses consensus mode, not majority vote.
stances.rhetorical_move: Four-factor structural-cause analysis of ASEAN paralysis.

stances.claim: Since the dispute is over interpretation and enforcement of UNCLOS, 'the way forward is to bring the conflicts among Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam to arbitration as provided precisely by Unclos. In my humble opinion, this is the best way forward under the rule of law.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Constructive-proposal close grounded in UNCLOS's own dispute-resolution mechanism.

notable_anecdotes.description: Three earlier maritime treaties whose boundaries are now superseded by UNCLOS compliance: the 1898 Treaty of Paris (US-Spain), the 1900 Treaty (US-Spain supplement), and the controversial 1930 US-UK treaty 'apparently delimiting the boundary between the Philippines and North Borneo.'
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Documents the legacy treaties the Philippines has chosen to override by current UNCLOS adherence.

notable_anecdotes.description: China's Unclos membership history: it identified with Third-World states protecting themselves from bigger powers during the 1973-1982 negotiations, joined the post-1971 UN recognition of the PRC vis-à-vis the Kuomintang-led Taiwan that 'was driven to Taiwan by the hordes of Mao Tse Tung,' ratified in 1996 with reservations -- but 'today, it has become a major military and economic power that no longer needs the protection of treaties to enforce its national interest. In fact, there is talk that the PRC is seriously thinking of withdrawing from Unclos.'
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Historical-strategic explanation of China's shifting Unclos relationship.

notable_anecdotes.description: ASEAN structural paralysis enumerated: (1) ASEAN is not a NATO-style military alliance; (2) Cambodia is not an Unclos member and is more inclined to side with China; (3) Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam have overlapping EEZ and CS claims among themselves; (4) ASEAN acts by consensus, not majority vote.
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Four-factor structural diagnosis of why ASEAN cannot unify against China.

notable_anecdotes.description: Two precedent dispute-settlement paths cited: PH-Indonesia disputes were settled diplomatically; Indonesia-Malaysia-Singapore brought their claims to the International Court of Justice.
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Concrete templates against which CJ proposes the arbitration alternative.

one_paragraph_summary: China's protest of the newly enacted Maritime Zones Act (RA 12064) and the Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act (RA 12065) is, in CJ Panganiban's framing, neither surprising nor warranted: the laws 'merely preserve and buttress our sovereign rights' under UNCLOS and the July 12, 2016 Arbitral Award issued by the Hague Permanent Court of Arbitration as registrar. RA 12064 defines the Philippine exclusive economic zone and continental shelf; RA 12065 designates the sea lanes and air routes foreign military and civilian aircraft/vessels may use within those zones. They clarify Article I of the 1987 Constitution's National Territory provision -- but by adopting UNCLOS-consistent boundaries, the Philippines voluntarily cedes some claims under the 1898 Treaty of Paris, the 1900 US-Spain supplement, and the controversial 1930 US-UK North Borneo treaty. CJ canvasses Unclos compliance asymmetry: 168 signatories; nine of ten ASEAN members signatories (Cambodia signed but did not ratify); China ratified in 1996 'with reservations' but 'has steadfastly claimed sovereignty over all the islands and islets, and maritime rights over almost the entire SCS under its nebulous nine-dash line theory (lately amended to 10-dash line) that had been invalidated by the Arbitral Award' -- enforced by 'more powerful and more numerous coast guard ships' patrolling 'with impunity' through 'laser guns, water cannons, ship boardings, and other gray zones tactics' under 'the old, old theory of discovery and conquest, a mode of acquiring title that has been overtaken by Unclos.' Why did China join Unclos in the first place? Because during the 1973-1982 negotiations the post-1971-UN-recognized PRC (vis-à-vis the Kuomintang-led Taiwan driven there 'by the hordes of Mao Tse Tung') identified itself with Third-World states needing treaty protection -- but today, as the world's number-two economy, it 'no longer needs the protection of treaties' and reportedly considers withdrawing. Why is the US not a member? Because the US Senate has refused ratification 'and will probably never ratify it' since the US prefers its actions 'governed only by its national interest, not by treaties' -- yet it enforces freedom of navigation under Unclos anyway. And why can't ASEAN unite against China? Four structural facts: ASEAN is not a NATO-style military alliance; Cambodia is not an Unclos member and aligns with China; Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam have overlapping EEZ/CS claims among themselves; and ASEAN operates by consensus, not majority vote. Past dispute-settlement paths include diplomacy (PH-Indonesia) and the ICJ (Indonesia-Malaysia-Singapore). CJ's recommended way forward: bring the Malaysia-Philippines-Vietnam overlap to arbitration under Unclos itself -- 'in my humble opinion, this is the best way forward under the rule of law.'
